title: Gladiator
synopsis: A general becomes a slave, becomes a gladiator, becomes the thing that an emperor cannot kill quietly.

nodes.text: Frost on the wheat stubble, and you walk the line rubbing grain between your fingers because it steadies your hands. Down the slope, the German emissary's head lies where they threw it, mouth open. Behind you, four thousand men stand in the trees with their spears grounded, breathing steam. Quintus asks whether you want the archers fired first or the catapults. The horns have not sounded yet.

choices.consequence: You send one rider forward under a branch of truce, and the Germans answer by shooting him out of the saddle in front of both armies.
You give the word and the treeline lights up with burning pitch, and the forest ahead of you starts screaming before the infantry has moved.

nodes.text: The tent smells of smoke and old man. Marcus Aurelius pours you wine with hands that shake and asks how many years since you saw your farm. Five, you tell him. He says the Republic was a good idea once and Rome has forgotten it, and that he wants you to hold the empire in trust until it can be handed back to the Senate. Outside, someone is grinding blades.

choices.consequence: You take the old man's hands and say yes, and by saying it you sign the death warrant of a wife you have not seen in five years.
You ask for the road home, the horses, the harvest, and he smiles and does not release you, and the offer stays lying there between you.

nodes.text: Commodus comes in still wearing his riding cloak, told nothing, expecting everything. He kneels for his father's blessing. The embrace goes on too long — long enough that you count it — and when the son stands, the old man is folded sideways in the chair with his mouth slack. Commodus turns around with wet eyes and asks you to be the first to grieve with him.

choices.consequence: You say the word father in the wrong tense and watch his face reset, and by nightfall your name is on a list held by men with short swords.
You bow, you say nothing, you leave the tent walking evenly, and he watches you all the way to the flap and understands you anyway.

nodes.text: They take you at first light in a clearing east of camp — Praetorians, not legionaries, city men in clean cloaks. One of them apologises. They cut your hands loose from the ropes only because a corpse is easier to carry unbound, and they tell you your family went ahead of you two days ago on the road south. Your sword is in the dirt three paces to your left.

choices.consequence: You get to the sword and four of them do not go home. It costs you a shoulder wound that will still ache in the arena a year from now.
You take a horse and ride south with your arm open to the bone, killing nothing, buying hours that turn out to be the wrong hours.

nodes.text: You smell it from a mile off and you know before you crest the ridge. The gate is broken inward. The olive trees are burning slowly, the way green wood does. Your wife and your son are hanging in the doorway of the house you built, and the ground under your horse comes up to meet your knees, and the horse walks away from you into the field.

choices.consequence: You dig two holes with a broken spear shaft and your bare hands and lay them down, and you are still on that ground when the slavers arrive.
You get four miles down the road before the fever from your shoulder puts you off the horse, and the tracks you were following go cold in the dust.

nodes.text: Proximo buys you in Zucchabar for the price of a good mule, chiefly because you are still alive. He was freed by an emperor's own hand once, he says, and he will tell you about it whether or not you ask. The yard is hard-packed dirt, a well, and thirty men who look at you and calculate. He tells you to win the crowd and you will win your freedom.

choices.consequence: You take the wooden practice sword and work until your palms tear open, and the other men stop calculating and start staying out of your way.
You put the wooden sword down in the dust and let them beat you for it, and Proximo has you flogged and fed and dragged out anyway.

nodes.text: Zucchabar's arena is a ring of packed earth with a market going on outside it. They chain you at the wrist to another man and push you both through a gate. The crowd is maybe six hundred people eating. A tall fighter with a curved blade circles you, and you can tell in three steps that he has been taught to entertain rather than to kill.

choices.consequence: You put him down in under four seconds with a chained arm and walk off, and the six hundred boo you for spoiling a morning's amusement.
You let it run long, take a cut across the ribs for the shape of it, and the market crowd stops eating and stands up to shout for you.

nodes.text: Your cell is a stone box that holds ten. The Numidian sleeps on his back with two small carved figures on his chest, a woman and a girl, whittled from a broken cart spoke. He wakes without moving and watches you scrape at the dirt floor with your thumbnail, making rows. Neither of you has said anything since the wagon. He offers you the water first.

choices.consequence: You tell him about a farm with a red roof and a stable door his hands could fit through, and he tells you the dead are only ahead of you.
You lie down facing the wall and say nothing, and he sets the water skin beside your head anyway and goes back to his carvings.

nodes.text: Proximo puts his ledger down. There are games in Rome for a hundred and fifty days straight, he says, paid for by an emperor who wants to be loved. The Colosseum swallows fifty thousand people. He wants you in it because you make money. You want it because there is exactly one man in the empire you need to stand close to, and he sits in a box above the sand.

choices.consequence: You tell Proximo you will go, and he studies your face for a long moment and decides not to ask why you agreed so fast.
You refuse, and he explains what happens to gladiators who refuse, and then he loads you onto the ship for Ostia in the morning regardless.

nodes.text: The announcer calls it the Fall of Carthage. They give you rusted mail and a shield with a split boss, and the gate lifts on a sand floor already raked flat. Chariots come out of the far tunnel with scythes bolted to the axles, and archers standing in the beds. The script has you as Carthage. Carthage is supposed to lose in the first few minutes.

choices.consequence: You go out alone at a dead run to break the chariot line and one wheel passes close enough to take the paint off your shield.
You bellow at strangers until they lock shields into a ring, spears outward, and the horses refuse the wall the way horses always do.

nodes.text: It ends faster than fifty thousand people paid for. The last chariot is on its side, the last man is face down, and the sand is very quiet. You turn a full circle with a sword in each hand and there is nobody left to fight. You shout at them — at all of them — and ask whether this is not what they came here for. The emperor's box is directly above you.

choices.consequence: You throw the sword up into the stands and it lands among senators, and fifty thousand Romans decide in one breath that they love you.
You lower your head and bend the neck, and the crowd cheers anyway, and Commodus comes down the stairs to meet a man who obeys.

nodes.text: He wants to know the name of the Spaniard the whole city is chanting for. A slave is not required to show his face to an emperor, but you take the helmet off with both hands and hold it against your hip, and you give him the full list — rank, legion, commander, husband, father — in the flat voice you used for reading casualty returns.

choices.consequence: You say your son's name and your wife's name out loud in front of fifty thousand witnesses, and Commodus cannot order your death without confessing everything.
You keep the helmet on and stand with your back straight and say nothing, and the silence tells him just as much, and the crowd fills it.

nodes.text: She comes down at night in a plain cloak, past guards who have been paid. Her hair is dressed for a banquet she left early. She says she wept when she heard, and you tell her that her brother slaughtered your family and she did nothing for two years. She puts her hand flat on the back of yours in the dark and says she has an army she cannot use.

choices.consequence: You turn your hand over and take hers, and you buy a conspiracy at the price of trusting a woman whose son is the next emperor.
You pull your hand back and tell her to leave, and she goes, and she keeps working on your behalf anyway without telling you a thing.

nodes.text: Gracchus arrives in the yard smelling of the baths, a senator visiting the animals. The plan is small and therefore plausible: a gate left open, a cart, the coast road, and five thousand legionaries at Ostia who still answer to your name. Two nights. After that Commodus moves the games and you lose the window. Behind him, through the bars, Lucius is watching you the way boys watch soldiers.

choices.consequence: You agree, and the senator leaves with your life in a wax tablet, and every man in that yard is now something Commodus can crucify.
You hesitate over a boy who reminds you of a boy in a doorway, and the delay costs the plot two nights it did not have.

nodes.text: Lucius is seven and wears a wooden sword on a belt made for a grown man. He calls you Maximus the Hero and recites your fights back to you in order, getting two of them wrong. His mother is not in the room. His uncle is, standing in the doorway with a cup in his hand, watching how gently a slave speaks to an heir.

choices.consequence: You kneel to his height and correct him about the chariots, and Commodus watches a child choose someone else's face and never forgets it.
You answer in three words and turn away, and the boy's face goes down, and the man in the doorway smiles because he understands cruelty.

nodes.text: They have not used tigers in years. The trapdoors are set in a ring and the handlers hold the chains just long enough. Across the sand is Tigris of Gaul, undefeated, retired, hauled out of comfortable old age in gold armor because the emperor needs someone to end you. The crowd is chanting a name and it is not his. He fights well. He fights like a man who has already lost.

choices.consequence: You put him on his knees, look up at the imperial box, and drop your blade in the sand while the whole Colosseum roars a word you did not choose.
You finish it clean and the crowd goes flat and disappointed, and Commodus finally has a reason to smile that costs him nothing.

nodes.text: A sewer runs under the Colosseum toward the river, and the air in it is warm and foul. Proximo's man has the gate. Two turns down, torchlight is coming the other way, moving in step, which is not how gladiators move. Behind you the passage back is full of men from your own yard with no weapons and no idea. The Praetorians have known about this tunnel for a day.

choices.consequence: You go forward into the torches with a stolen gladius and open a way out for exactly one man, and the tunnel behind you fills with screaming.
You turn back for men who have no blades, which is what a general does, and the Praetorians take the whole yard in the dark.

nodes.text: Proximo is at the gate in a good cloak with his freedom papers on him, and he has your Spanish sword wrapped in cloth under his arm. He hands it over. He says shadows and dust, the way he always does, and then he sets his feet in the gateway with a short blade against eight Praetorians, which buys you one flight of stairs.

choices.consequence: You take the sword and go, and behind you an old showman finally gets the death he has been rehearsing in that yard for twenty years.
You plant yourself beside him and they take you both, and every plan Rome had for a free Republic dies in a doorway with two old men.

nodes.text: They bring her into the cell with her wrists tied and her chin up. Commodus stands behind her with the point of a knife resting on the shoulder seam of her dress, and Lucius is somewhere upstairs asleep in a room with a guard outside it. He explains it patiently, like arithmetic. He wants a public death in the arena and he wants you to walk to it without struggling.

choices.consequence: You put your hands out for the irons and she says your name once, and the sound of it is the only thing you take down to the sand.
You go for his throat across the cell and four men put you on the floor, and the knife opens a line on her shoulder that he will never apologise for.

nodes.text: One lamp lights the armory under the arena. He comes down in white, alone except for the men holding your arms, and talks about legacy while he works the blade in under your ribs from behind, low, where the breastplate straps close over it. They buckle the armor on top. He tells the guards to strap it tight. Above you, fifty thousand people are already stamping.

choices.consequence: You keep your breathing shallow and your left arm down and walk out onto the sand with a lie held shut under bronze plating.
You start to pull the strap loose to show the crowd what he did, and Quintus quietly puts a hand over yours and shakes his head.

nodes.text: The floor is fresh sand and the light is enormous. He circles you in white and gold and tells the crowd this is between brothers. Your left side is filling up with something warm. Every step you take leaves a print that darkens after you have left it. The Colosseum, all of it, has gone silent enough that you can hear his boots turning, and he still thinks he is winning.

choices.consequence: You take the blade off his wrist and put it through his throat in one motion, and Rome hears a sword come out of an emperor.
You let the sword fall out of your hand and ask the Praetorians for theirs, and every one of them stands still and does not move.
You do neither. You take his weapon, look at Quintus, and hand the whole question of Rome to a man who has been waiting to be asked.

nodes.text: The wheat comes up past your hands and the sun is on the back of your neck for the first time in six years. There is a gate ahead with a rope latch you tied yourself, badly, and never fixed. You push it open. A boy is running down the row toward you and behind him a woman is standing in the doorway with flour on her forearms, and she says your name the way it was always meant to be said.

Gracchus and four gladiators carry your body up out of the sand and the crowd parts for it without being told. In the weeks after, the Senate meets more than it has in a decade and something like debate happens in the open air. It does not last. But for a season, laws are written by men who argue, and a boy grows up in a palace hearing that his uncle lost.

Juba comes back at night when the Colosseum is empty and the sand has been raked. He kneels at the spot and digs with his fingers until the hole is deep enough for two small figures cut from a cart spoke. He covers them over and presses the sand flat with his palm. Then he stands and tells the empty seats that he will see you again — but not yet. Not yet.
